title: Access methods
lead: Sequential scans, composite search keys, index-only scans and bitmap access.

sections.title: Sequential scans and index selection
sections.html:
Scan cursor and selectivity

An access path retrieves base tuples and may apply predicates. A sequential scan iterates every page, fetches it through the buffer pool and tests live tuples, retaining a cursor for resume. It reads N source pages even if only sel(p) of tuples qualify.

sel(p)·N is an approximate packed output-page count only when widths and packing match. It is not a formula for source pages skipped. On-the-fly output avoids intermediate writes but cannot avoid reading pages merely because their tuples later fail the predicate.

PDF pp. 1–3

Choosing one candidate index

For age<30 AND dept='CS' AND country='UK', the source considers an age tree and a dept index. If99 rows meet age but only2 meet dept, start from dept candidates; with the counts reversed, age may be cheaper. The unindexed country term remains a residual test.

Cost also depends on clustering, index traversal, tuple widths and needed output attributes; matching fewer index entries is only one factor. Trees support equality/ranges; hashing supports equality on the complete hashed key. Multiple predicates do not imply a single index can narrow all of them.

PDF pp. 4–6

sections.title: Composite keys and lexicographic ranges
sections.html:
Composite-key ordering

IDNameAgeSalary
123Jones31300
443Smith32400
244Gold55140
134Alvaro55400
221McDonald79300

Index(Age,Salary) sorts Age first and Salary within equal Age. A direct contiguous lookup binds a leading equality prefix and optionally ranges over the next column. Later-column conditions can filter entries but do not in general define one tighter contiguous interval.

Changing key order changes supported prefixes. The displayed ages/salaries are the source data; no added page/RID story is needed to explain this property.

PDF pp. 7–9

Results of every source predicate

PredicateMatchesContiguous prefix range?
Age = 31 AND Salary = 400noneyes, empty lookup
Age = 55 AND Salary > 200Alvaroyes
Age > 31 AND Salary = 400Smith, Alvaronot one exact interval
Age = 31Jonesyes
Age > 31Smith, Gold, Alvaro, McDonaldyes
Salary = 300Jones, McDonaldno leading Age bound

Age>31 can scan the age suffix but must reject Gold and McDonald for Salary=400. Salary=300 is scattered across ages; a broad scan or specialised strategy is needed. A predicate yielding no matches can still be a valid index lookup.

PDF pp. 10–15

sections.title: Index-only, clustered and hash scans
sections.html:
Index-only examples and their required fields

Employee(dno) entries can support GROUP BY dno,COUNT(*) because each qualifying index entry contributes one employee. (dno,salary) supports per-department MIN(salary); (age,salary) supports AVG(salary) WHERE age=25 AND salary>300. All requested and filtering fields must be present.

An index storing only age and RID cannot supply another output field such as name. Real MVCC engines may still consult heap visibility information even when projected fields are covered. Covering data and visibility are separate conditions for an actual index-only execution.

PDF p. 16

Clustered versus unclustered scan ledgers

A tree scan pays descent (about2–4 I/Os in the source), matching leaf reads and, for referenced entries, matching data-page fetches. Clustered data often costs approximately sel(p)·N data reads; unclustered data can approach one per matching entry.

Index-only access avoids the data-fetch term regardless of heap clustering. For many unclustered matches, sort RIDs by page before fetching so several tuple references share one page read. Count distinct pages separately from number of tuples; caching and reordering determine whether repeated requests cause physical I/O.

PDF pp. 17–18

Composite hash lookup

A hash index on(age,dept) can directly locate age=27 AND dept='CS', because both hashed components are known. age=27 alone does not determine the combined hash. A tree on the same ordered columns can use its leading age prefix, which illustrates a fundamental difference between hash and tree access.

Inspect every relevant bucket/overflow entry for nonunique keys; stop after the found match only when uniqueness permits. Residual predicates and referenced-record fetches still apply.

PDF p. 19

sections.title: Multi-index and bitmap scans
sections.html:
RID combinations, bitmaps and the restricted exercise

For age<30 AND dept='CS', intersect RID sets from the two indexes, fetch candidates and check country='UK'. OR can union complete candidate sets. Exact bitmaps/hash sets compute exact combinations; Bloom filters can prefilter but require verification because of false positives.

PostgreSQL separates Bitmap Index Scan (build candidate positions) from Bitmap Heap Scan (visit heap pages, fetch/recheck rows). Grouping candidates by page reduces random access. The source practice uses Bay Area Bike Sharing from restricted Learn worksheets and EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The public slide describes its objective and plan operators; it does not supply the missing worksheet data or establish that PostgreSQL measurements were run here.

PDF pp. 20–23

quiz.question: Which predicate forms a contiguous range in an index on (A,B)?
options: B=20 with any value of A
A>7 AND B=20 with no residual check needed at all
quiz.explanation: An equality prefix on A followed by a range on B forms one contiguous interval in the index.
